item.title: Three New Pieces For Fall
item.dc:creator: Roseland
item.content:encoded:
To our friends and customers,

Today we have three new additions to Roseland. They are well suited to this time of year, though that was not intentional!

Our glass hurricanes are mouth-blown by Asher Holman in Asheville, using silica from Spruce Pine, North Carolina. Their shape is drawn from an early nineteenth-century example in the Met’s collection, though it’s as familiar a form as you might expect. We also added a glass base to hold a taper candle. There are small bubbles and ripples in the glass, and slight variations in shape from working it by hand.

Our new sideboard takes its cues from the same 1825 Shaker double counter that inspired our dressers. Those have become some of our most-loved pieces, and we wanted to adapt them for the kitchen and dining room: a 36-inch counter height, undermount soft-close drawers and a choice of widths.

As with our dressers, each drawer front is a single board of cherry or walnut. It gives you a long, uninterrupted stretch of grain to look at, with just linseed oil rubbed into the wood. The drawer boxes are dovetailed white pine. If the height suits, there’s no reason it shouldn’t also be a dresser.

And lastly, we’re finally releasing the loveseat version of our Rolled Arm Sofa. It’s the same form and materials but in a more intimate size. For customer owned textiles, the required yardage is 15 yards.

Thank you for being a customer. As always, if you have any questions about any of these, anything on our site, or just an existing Roseland item you own, please just respond to this email and we’ll get in touch. In the future, we will be using Substack’s email tool to send our new product emails. Pictures of all the pieces are below.

Best,

Luke

item.title: Introducing the Russel Wright Collection
item.dc:creator: Roseland
item.content:encoded:
To our friends and customers,

Today we’re excited to introduce the Russel Wright Collection.

Russel and Mary Wright were among the most influential American designers of the twentieth century. Their vision of modern American life was informal and practical, with a lasting place for natural materials and things made by hand. It’s a vision we share at Roseland.

In 1940, Russel chose Old Hickory furniture for his “Outdoor Living Room” at The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Soon after, he designed his own collection for Old Hickory, bringing modern forms to their traditional bent-hickory and woven-splint construction. More than eighty years later, we’ve worked with Manitoga, The Russel Wright Design Center, and Old Hickory to bring three of those designs back into production: the Arm Chair, Low Lounge Chair, and Chaise Lounge.

Each chair is made by hand at Old Hickory’s workshop in Indiana using techniques practiced for generations. The frames are solid hickory, steam-bent and shaped, with seats and backs woven by hand in rattan. What we particularly like is how directly the materials become the furniture: the bent hickory gives the chairs their shape, and the woven rattan forms the surfaces you sit against. They are finished with hand-rubbed tung oil and a small amount of natural burnt umber pigment.

We photographed the collection at Manitoga, the Wrights’ home and studio in Garrison, New York, now preserved as a center for his work and ideas. You can see photos below and view the collection here or at our office in New York. You can schedule an appointment to see them here.

We’re very grateful to everyone at Manitoga and Old Hickory who helped make this possible. It means a lot to us to be able to share a small part of Wright’s work with you.

Best,

Luke Sherwin

item.title: Our Armchair is here
item.description: Hello, Today we’re pleased to introduce two new pieces to Roseland: our Rolled Arm Chair and a Round Candle Stand.
item.dc:creator: Roseland
item.content:encoded:
Hello,

Today we’re pleased to introduce two new pieces to Roseland: our Rolled Arm Chair and a Round Candle Stand.

The Rolled Arm Chair follows our Rolled Arm Sofa, sharing the same approach to proportion, construction, and natural materials. Its low arms let your shoulders relax, and the curved back supports your lumbar. One historic detail that we particularly like is the way the seat converges towards the rear, cradling your hips as you sit. It’s a small bit of geometry that has a lot to do with how it both looks and feels. It is made in North Carolina by Vanguard Furniture.

It’s currently available in a cream, American-woven 100% cotton twill, or upholstered in eight yards of your own fabric. We’re also planning Belgian linen slipcovers and additional fabric options by the end of the year. The slipcovers will fit chairs purchased now, so you’ll have the option to change the covering later.

The Round Candle Stand is a side table modeled on a late 18th-century piece in our collection. Each one is made by Jeff Puls in Missouri, using a single stave of solid cherry for the post and is finished by hand with linseed oil.

Thank you, as always, for following along. If you have any questions, do reply to this email (this is automated, but my response won’t be).

Best,

Luke Sherwin (owner)

item.title: Introducing a Wide Board Oak Table
item.dc:creator: Roseland
item.content:encoded:
To our friends and customers,

I’m excited to introduce our Wide Board Oak Table: a solid, Appalachian-grown, white-oak dining table modeled on eighteenth-century farmhouse tables and made with individual boards between seven and twelve inches wide.

Often called the “King of Hardwoods,” American white oak is dense, heavy, rot-resistant, and effortlessly beautiful. Like many of our most desirable native species, its history is one of slow recovery. Today, the tree’s biomass is growing nationally, as well as in West Virginia.

The table was inspired by our love of early American white-oak farm tables. There’s a sense of lost abundance in the huge boards they used, and a primitive repairability to their structure. There were no spray booths, polyurethanes, or veneers, and “white oak” meant white oak, rather than a named stain applied to another species. A couple hundred years later, it’s often the patina of indentations and use marks that makes these antique tables even more desirable.

Our design is an attempt to bring the past back into the present. Each tabletop is assembled from only four or five boards, each measuring seven to twelve inches wide and a full inch thick. Good boards at the upper end of that range are uncommon. Using so few allows the grain to travel across the table with unusual breadth and calm. If one’s goal is to pass down furniture, wide white oak is about as good as it gets.

The table is made by Caperton Furnitureworks in Berkeley Springs, West Virginia. Each one is finished by hand with Odie’s Oil, a food-safe, solvent-free hard-wax oil, and pure raw linseed oil. Both are zero-VOC finishes. This natural finish leaves the wood feeling like wood and allows rings, scratches, and blemishes to be repaired locally with light sanding and a two-minute reapplication of oil. We believe the years will add to the table rather than diminish it.

The Wide Board Oak Table is available now in 72-, 84-, 96-, and 108-inch lengths. Because of the efficient leg placement, the two shorter sizes seat eight, while the two longer sizes seat ten. Prices begin at $2,375, with $195 white-glove delivery and assembly throughout the lower 48.

You’ll find photos below, including photos of our forthcoming White Oak Windsor Chairs. As always, we are grateful for your continued support of Roseland.

Best,

Luke Sherwin

Owner

item.title: Roseland’s First Sofa
item.dc:creator: Roseland
item.content:encoded:
To our friends and customers,

After more than a year in development, we’re very excited to introduce our first upholstered piece: the Rolled Arm Sofa.

I’ve always loved the rolled arm because it’s elegant and comfortable. When done right, its low arms allow your shoulders to relax, its curved back offers a little lumbar support, and proud cushions call you to sit down.

The rolled arm’s lineage runs through Howard & Sons, the nineteenth-century London upholstery house whose work helped define the English tradition of deeply comfortable, structurally sophisticated seating. In 1866, George Howard patented the “Elastic Seat,” an early recognition that comfort begins with structure.

Since then, the rolled arm has become part of American living – in libraries, hotels, parlors, and homes across the country. But in the last 50 years, designs have drifted away from the classic. They’ve become deeper, flatter, bulkier, and filled with polyurethane foam.

At Roseland, we wanted to recover the proportions and materials that gave the original sofa its enduring appeal. We designed the sofa with particular focus on the delicate, tapering curves of the arm, mirrored those lines with the base of the sofa, and restored posture to the back. We partnered with Vanguard Furniture in North Carolina to develop a handmade solid-maple frame with white oak or walnut legs, eight-way hand-tied springs, burlap seat deck, and wool trim padding. The cushions combine 95:5 traceable American feather and down with three-inch organic latex cores, giving them softness, loft, and resilience without chemical fill. When you sit on the sofa, you slowly sink into it, and when you get up, you’ll leave behind a faint impression of your bottom.

For fabrics, we’re intentionally starting small. The sofa is available in a cream cotton twill woven in America, or it can be upholstered in a textile of your choosing through our Customer’s Own Material program.

The Rolled Arm Sofa is available now in 84-inch and 96-inch lengths. It will start shipping in September. An armchair and loveseat will follow this fall.

You’ll find photos below. We’re very proud of this one, and grateful for your continued support of Roseland.

Best,

Clare de Boer, Owner

P.S. We’ve opened a small office at 255 Canal Street in Manhattan, where most of our pieces, including the sofa, are available to sit on and see (2nd picture below). To arrange a visit, simply reply to this email and we’ll set up an appointment. Looking forward to having you in.

item.title: Introducing The Wave Hill Chair
item.dc:creator: Roseland
item.content:encoded:
To our friends and customers,

Today we’re pleased to introduce the Wave Hill Chair, our second outdoor chair and the first made in partnership with Wave Hill.

The chair takes its cues from a garden seat found on the grounds at Wave Hill, a majestic Bronx estate looking across the Hudson toward New Jersey’s Palisades. It descends from Gerrit Rietveld’s 1918 Red and Blue Chair and Lester Collins’ 1960s outdoor adaptation for Innisfree in Millbrook, New York. The design beautifully balances architectural formality with an at-ease posture.

Our version is made from solid American white oak, grown in Pennsylvania, and assembled with threaded inserts for a long life in the elements. It is finished by hand with a penetrating juniper waterproofer as well as pure raw tung oil grown in Florida. Like our Westport Chair, it will gracefully silver with age, or you can apply a pigmented finish of your choosing (we love pine tar for this purpose).

The chair is comfortable for long afternoons and belongs almost anywhere: on a porch, beneath a tree, beside a garden path, or facing the last light of day.

Pricing starts at $595 for one, with progressive savings for multiple chairs. The chair ships free via UPS Ground directly from Kenon Perry’s workshop in Bosque County, Texas. Assembly is straightforward, taking about 15 minutes per chair. We include the necessary Allen key in the box.

Four percent of revenues from each chair will support Wave Hill and its ongoing stewardship of one of New York City’s great public landscapes.

Thank you, as always, for supporting Roseland.

Best,
Luke Sherwin and Clare de Boer
Owners

item.title: Designing the Roseland Bed
item.description: How early American furniture shaped the design of our first bed.
item.dc:creator: Roseland
item.content:encoded:
Our vision for the Roseland bed was to create something so classic that it would feel familiar. We wanted to do this by being loyal to early American design but with new contributions that would be useful and original.

To create the bed, we partnered with Kenon Perry, a veteran furniture designer and maker, with a career in NYC, Atlanta, and now Bosque County, Texas. Kenon, like us, appreciated the visual paradox of many 18th and early 19th century beds: a planted, rock-solid construction contrasted with long, tapering, visually delicate legs. Like countless others before us, the stark, unadorned, lines of the Shakers were the natural starting point.

For inspiration, we visited the Hancock Shaker Village and scoured the Met’s design archive for the different approaches to supports, headboards, and joinery.

In the end, the bed we designed has a few features that make it different to its ancestral beds as well as its contemporary peers:

“We wanted to create something that was so simple and timeless, that it would feel almost familiar.”

Uniform leg tapering - We wanted something strong yet visually light. By turning the bed legs with a simplified linear reduction in thickness, the bed has the appearance of standing on needlepoints while maintaining a strong structure. We mirrored this in the headboard posts and center support.

We created a reversible headboard connection. As the facade of the bed and the true showcase of the wood’s grain - designing a tight, durable headboard connection was always a goal. Most headboards connect to the vertical supports with visible screw holes on the side of the headboard facing the wall. This has two consequences that we wanted to avoid: Firstly, if the face-side of the headboard gets damaged, you can’t flip it around. Secondly, it avoids the small stress fractures that can occur over time in the wood around the screw holes. The Roseland headboard is two sided, so a customer can choose their preferred side and locks in place using Mod-eez - an Austrian connector that is celebrated by high-end furniture makers for its tight, fully concealed hold - our one concession to imports!

A natural, zero-VOC finish. With our commitment to finishing all of our products as naturally as possible (forgoing lacquers, stains, synthetic polymers, or veneers), we opted to hand-rub pure linseed oil as our only finish. This provides a long lasting and repairable finish to the bed - if a customer blemishes or dings the bed, they can just sand and re-apply linseed oil.
